KEY MESSAGE 1...Advisory-level heat builds into the region starting 
tomorrow and lingering through Friday. The heat and humidity help to 
fuel the chance for widely scattered thunderstorms Thursday and 
Friday afternoon.

Heat and humidity ramp up Thursday as return flow around sprawling 
subtropical high pressure advects a warm and humid air mass into the 
region. By Thursday morning, the most noticeable change will be in 
humidity values as dew point temperatures surge into the low 70s 
across the area. Still seeing guidance paint a broad area of very 
warm 925 mb temperatures on the order of +22-26C Thursday and 
Friday. These very warm low level temperatures translate to highs in 
the upper 80s to mid 90s. Combined with near oppressive dew points 
of 72-76, apparent temperatures will climb to the upper 90s, 
possibly near 100 at times. Greatest risk of heat indicies >100 will 
be found in the CT and Merrimack River Valleys where localized 
downslope winds likely help boost temperatures. Some uncertainty as 
to the magnitude of heat elsewhere resulting from cloud cover from 
any thunderstorms that develop Thursday and Friday afternoons. 
Still, at a minimum heat index values will likely reach or exceed 95 
for most locations both Thursday and Friday afternoons. Finally, 
elevated overnight temps in the low to mid 70s paired with elevated 
dew points keeping heat indicies near 80 overnight. The warm 
overnight temperatures will be dangerous for those without adequate 
access to cooling, especially in urban areas. 

Regarding the thunderstorm potential later in the week... a few 
weak, upper level disturbances passing through New England combining 
with the high heat/humidity and just enough instability will likely 
be enough to pop a few diurnal showers/thunderstorms each day 
Thursday through the weekend, with greatest chances across the 
interior on Thursday. Any thunderstorms that do pop have the 
potential to produce frequent lightning, gusty winds, and torrential 
downpours as PWATs will likely be around 2.0". Given the amount of 
rain southern New England has seen over the last week or so, any 
heavy downpours could lead to localized flooding.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Midsummer warmth and humidity continue across much 
of southern New England through the weekend. Afternoon pop-up 
thunderstorms are most likely Saturday, with a lower chance on 
Sunday. Unsettled weather may return early next week, although 
confidence remains low in the exact details.

Confidence remains high that midsummer warmth and humidity will 
continue through this weekend, along with daily chances for 
afternoon pop-up thunderstorms. Of the two weekend days, Saturday 
appears to have the greater probability of showers and 
thunderstorms. However, a widespread washout is not anticipated. 
Given the abundant rainfall earlier this week, any storms capable of 
producing heavy downpours could lead to localized instances of flash 
flooding. This is reflected in the WPC Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 4) 
for excessive rainfall across western New England on Saturday.

There is little change in the synoptic pattern, with Bermuda high 
pressure remaining anchored over the western Atlantic. Persistent 
southwesterly flow will continue to advect above-normal temperatures 
and increasing humidity into southern New England through the 
weekend. While temperatures will remain above climatological 
normals, they are not particularly unusual for early August. High 
temperatures Saturday and Sunday should climb into the upper 80s to 
around 90 degrees, while dewpoints remain in the lower 70s. 
Overnight lows in the 70s will provide little relief. This 
combination will result in daytime heat index values of 90 to 95 
degrees, which is below Heat Advisory criteria and is why the 
current advisory does not extend into Saturday. Another uncertainty 
is the degree of afternoon cloud cover and thunderstorm development, 
which could temper temperatures somewhat. Forecast trends will 
continue to be monitored to determine whether the Heat Advisory will 
need to be extended into Saturday. Temperatures trend somewhat lower 
Monday into Tuesday as cloud cover increases and the potential for 
more widespread shower activity develops.

Regarding thunderstorm chances, the mid-level ridge offshore 
gradually flattens, resulting in a more zonal flow aloft. Embedded 
shortwave disturbances moving through the flow should provide 
sufficient lift to initiate scattered afternoon and evening 
thunderstorms on Saturday and potentially again on Sunday, although 
Sunday currently appears to be the drier of the two weekend days. 
While deep-layer shear remains weak, with 0-6 km bulk shear 
generally below 30 kt, instability will be plentiful, with forecast
